title: Prediction Markets Aren't Casinos, but 90% of Volume Comes from Sports
dek: Kalshi spent four years on compliance to win 90% market share, but its revenue structure looks more like a sportsbook; what's truly undervalued are quiet markets like FDA approvals.
why: The first half is founder narrative; the real value is in the middle and later sections: how contracts are written, sports making up 90%, and regulatory risk. Worth listening for anyone wanting to understand prediction market mechanics.
who: Founders and investors interested in prediction markets, regulatory arbitrage, and information aggregation mechanisms; those wanting to understand Kalshi's business model and compliance path.
skip: The opening historical setup about Greek oracles, Andean potato farmers, and the Iowa Electronic Markets can be fast-forwarded.

points.h: Comply for four years first, then open the first market
points.body: Kalshi's two founders wrote "regulatory first" into the company's principles, spending four years to get regulatory approval before launching their first market. Mansoor says this is anti-Silicon Valley: others build the product first and patch compliance later, but they asked the federal government first, "How should this be regulated?" The cost was nearly giving up almost every day for the first four years, sustained by "the cost of regret is too high." The result: in 2024, a federal appeals court ruled Kalshi could list election contracts, landing just before the presidential election. Mansoor attributes their 90% market share directly to this path: institutions prefer to plug into a platform inside the system, because changing the rules from outside is harder.

points.h: Prediction markets force you to shut up, not to take a stance
points.body: Robin Hanson gives three mechanisms for why prediction markets are more accurate than polls or expert interviews. First, interviewees have incentives to be interesting, dramatic, and to please the questioner, while the market only rewards being right. Second, the market gives you an incentive to shut up about topics you don't understand—you'll only bet on the few markets where you truly have an edge, whereas interviewees will answer even if they don't know. Third, the market doesn't require you to have a direct opinion on a topic; it invites you to find biases and errors in others' pricing, and pays you to correct them. He closes with an old poker table saying: sit down and first find the sucker; if you can't find one, the sucker is you, so don't play this market.

points.h: Internal prediction markets die from project leaders' excuses
points.body: Eli Lilly ran an internal prediction market in the early 2000s that successfully predicted which drug compounds would pass Phase III trials; Google also had a project called Google Profit. Both were considered effective but neither survived. Hanson's explanation: project leaders want to know if they can deliver on time, but they want even more a good excuse if they fail. And the best excuse is precisely "we were on track, but at the last minute an unforeseen accident happened." A market that consistently and accurately predicts "will you be late?" would invalidate that excuse in advance, so no one wants it to exist.

points.h: Domain expertise is not the key ability for predicting the future
points.body: Mansoor cites Philip Tetlock's Superforecasting research: when experts in a domain (e.g., geopolitics) are pitted against a group of non-experts predicting the same set of events, the non-experts win. His explanation is that domain experts become too dogmatic over time, while those who can step back and look at problems calmly have better self-calibration and fewer biases. Mansoor says this is quite heretical in political, academic, and financial analysis circles—it means that to get more accurate answers, you should seek a diverse group of participants who pride themselves on self-calibration, critical reading, and filtering information, rather than an authority in a specific field. He treats this as Kalshi's underlying logic.

points.h: Writing one contract takes a month, for grammar and apostrophes
points.body: Nicole Kagan is responsible for writing contracts and self-certifying them with the CFTC. The most complex category is "what someone will say in a certain speech." They recently rewrote the rules because a bunch of grammar issues came up: what if an apostrophe appears? If a word is said wrong or mispronounced, does it still count as the same word? What if it appears in a proper noun? What if the live stream cuts out and is later uploaded elsewhere? These rules took over a month to write, seven or eight pages, extremely detailed. When Bloomberg reported, they guessed these rules were for automated processing and must be for AI; Kagan says absolutely not—they were written so users could understand, and they never considered that "what a human can understand, a computer probably can too."

points.h: When you can't judge a winner, settle at the last fair price
points.body: Kalshi's contracts are usually binary: pay $1 if the event happens, $0 if not, with each position fully collateralized—if one side bets 30 cents, someone must bet 70 cents. But some situations can't be judged yes or no. Cardi B was clearly dancing in her seven-second Super Bowl halftime show cameo, but she wasn't wearing a mic and it was impossible to confirm whether she was singing; the team said "we are epistemologically uncertain," so they settled at the last fair price. Another case is 50-50: when multiple people win simultaneously, each settles at 50 cents. Kagan says they have the right to do this when it's "really unclear" whether an event meets the criteria, and they have already revised the halftime show contract—the new rules require an audible lead or backing vocal, and under the new rules Cardi B is considered not to have performed.

points.h: 90% of volume comes from sports, the most uncomfortable fact
points.body: Dubner directly points out: about 90% of Kalshi's volume is concentrated in a category barely mentioned before—sports, the business that makes DraftKings and FanDuel nervous. Mansoor's response is that the sports share is falling rapidly and other categories are growing faster, but he admits "10% is also big, don't forget we're large." He insists on distinguishing gambling from trading: all derivatives markets are primarily speculative, speculation provides liquidity, and the key is not whether there is speculation but the business model—one model specifically seeks out losers and bans winners, the other pursues price discovery and wants smart people to come in. He also acknowledges the second model has risks, saying there is "responsible gambling" and "responsible trading," and platforms have a responsibility to monitor.

points.h: 70-80% of active users never place a trade
points.body: Mansoor says one of his favorite numbers is: 70% to 80% of active users don't trade; they just log in every day, put it next to X and a few newspapers, and use it to calibrate or verify information. Kalshi's business model is a neutral platform, like the NYSE or Nasdaq, taking an average 1% on trades and not caring who wins or loses. He also says the information environment is becoming more polarized and the signal-to-noise ratio is declining, because social media algorithms reward clickbait: a nuanced, restrained, multi-paragraph opinion gets only four likes on X, while something extreme and outrageous gets tens of thousands; prediction markets have exactly the opposite incentive—that nuanced, boring, well-calibrated judgment is the one that makes money.
